title: How Alchemy Worked
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck (the transcript labels him "iHeart Intro" in places) trace alchemy from its roots in ancient China, India, Egypt and Hellenistic Greece through the Arab world and into medieval Europe, covering its goals of immortality, gold-making and the Philosopher's Stone, key figures such as Zosimos of Panopolis, Jabir, Rhazes, Albertus Magnus, Paracelsus, Nicholas Flamel and Isaac Newton, and its legacy for chemistry and the scientific method. The episode closes with a listener correction about the heavy metal documentary Heavy Metal Parking Lot.
topics: Stuff You Should Know listener mail

entities.name: Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone

segments.title: Opening
segments.summary: Brief iHeart intro and the hosts' opening banter about the episode's theme of alchemy.

segments.title: Popular image of alchemy and its reputation
segments.summary: The hosts describe the popular image of alchemists as robed magicians and charlatans, and argue that alchemists were more interesting than history suggests and laid groundwork for modern chemistry and the scientific method.

segments.title: Origins in China and immortality elixirs
segments.summary: Alchemy's early purpose was an elixir of immortality, pursued in China by Taoists who mixed mercury, arsenic and sulfur, with many deaths likely. Accidental discoveries included potassium nitrate (gunpowder) and ammonium chloride. Chinese alchemy declined as Buddhism spread.

segments.title: India and the value of gold
segments.summary: Indian alchemy focused more on health and disease cures, and gold was revered as the best metal, which led to gold-making associations.

segments.title: Egypt, Greece and Hellenistic alchemy
segments.summary: After Alexander the Great invaded Egypt in 322 BCE, Greek thinkers combined their philosophy, physics and astrology with Egyptian alchemy. The hosts note early experimental attitudes.

segments.title: Bolos of Mendes and Hermes Trismegistus
segments.summary: Bolos of Mendes wrote around 200 BCE what is considered the first preserved alchemical writing on making gold and silver. Medieval monks attributed alchemical texts to the legendary Hermes Trismegistus, a syncretic figure combining Thoth and Hermes.

segments.title: Zosimos of Panopolis and definition of alchemy
segments.summary: Zosimos of Panopolis wrote many books on alchemy and gave a definition of the field as the study of the composition of waters, movement, growth and the bonding of spirits within bodies. He credited methods to a Jewish woman named Maria, which may have influenced the water bath used in cooking.

segments.title: Aristotle's four elements and atoms
segments.summary: The hosts explain that early alchemy worked within Aristotle's four-element framework, which later science saw as a wrong turn, while Democritus had proposed atoms.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Arab world alchemy and transmission to Europe
segments.summary: Arab scholars took up alchemy, with theories about basic qualities of heat, cold, dryness and moisture, and figures like Rhazes and Jabir, sometimes called the father of chemistry, made methodical contributions. Texts were translated into Arabic and then Latin, spreading into Europe around the twelfth century, possibly via the Crusades.

segments.title: European alchemy, elixirs and Philosopher's Stone
segments.summary: European scholars experimented with mineral acids and elixirs. The hosts discuss the Philosopher's Stone as the perfect substance that would turn base metals into gold, and the idea that metals naturally progress toward gold.

segments.title: Albertus Magnus, Jean de Roquetaillade and Arnaud de Villeneuve's distillation
segments.summary: Albertus Magnus studied Arab and Greek alchemy. Franciscan monk Jean de Roquetaillade sought gold to fund the Church, despite a vow of poverty. The hosts discuss the alchemists' motives beyond greed, such as ending poverty and disease. A physician distilled wine into aqua vitae, the quintessence, and claimed it preserved meat.

segments.title: Paracelsus
segments.summary: Paracelsus, born Philippus Theophrastus Aureolus Bombastus von Hohenheim, is described as coining that the dose makes the poison, promoting secrecy about alchemy, and questioning Galen's four humors theory of disease.

segments.title: Nicholas Flamel legend
segments.summary: Nicholas Flamel is credited with a book that supposedly revealed the Philosopher's Stone after 21 years of translation. Later alchemists created a legend that he made the stone and got rich, though his wife's wealth is the likely explanation. He endowed hospitals, schools and churches, and his age at death is uncertain, recorded between 80 and 114.

segments.title: Homunculi and the Book of the Cow
segments.summary: Alchemists tried to create homunculi, artificial miniature humans, to study how life begins. The hosts describe a recipe in the Book of the Cow, an Arabic ninth-century text, and exchange jokes about Happy Days and sheep.

segments.title: Brady Bunch goat and transition to legacy
segments.summary: The hosts recall a Brady Bunch episode with a stolen goat, then recap alchemy's modern reputation and its contributions to metallurgy and medicine.

segments.title: Alchemy's contribution to the scientific method and chemistry
segments.summary: The hosts argue alchemists were the first to work in labs with measured materials and record results, forming basic outlines of the scientific method. The word chemistry derives from alchemy, and romantic chemistry predates scientific chemistry by about two centuries.

segments.title: Isaac Newton and alchemy
segments.summary: Isaac Newton pursued alchemy alongside physics, believing it was divine wisdom given to humans. His alchemy papers were kept private for centuries. A biographer called him the last alchemist rather than the first scientist.

segments.title: Royal patronage and the Academy
segments.summary: Holy Roman Emperors Maximilian II and Rudolph II financially supported alchemists. England's Henry VI licensed alchemists and minted alchemical gold coins. The Académie Royale des Sciences in 1666 dropped alchemy from its scientific pursuits.

segments.title: Alchemy's reputation and science's disavowal
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how alchemy later became associated with fraud, and how science disavowed its predecessors, while now treating alchemy as a grandfather of modern chemistry.

segments.title: Grandfather banter and music tangent
segments.summary: Casual banter about grandfathers and a mention of the Dungeon synth band Witch Bolt, which the hosts recommend.

segments.title: Pre-mail wrap-up
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up the alchemy topic and introduce listener mail. They also mention High Mage Productions jingles sent by a listener.

segments.title: Listener correction on Heavy Metal Parking Lot
segments.summary: Listener Matthew T from Cleveland, Ohio corrects Chuck: Heavy Metal Parking Lot was made by Jeff Krulik and John Heyn, not Penelope Spheeris, who made Decline of the Western Civilization. He also mentions their documentary Neil Diamond Parking Lot.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank the listener and explain how to submit mail, and the iHeart closing plays.
